subtopics.title: Sorting the Moves — A Vocabulary for Migration

questions.question: A nurse commuting to a night shift and a family on holiday are NOT migrants because:
options: They travel too slowly
Their place of residence does not change — their movement is circulation
They do not cross a provincial boundary
They travel in groups

questions.question: The three axes used to classify migration are:
options: Age, income and education of the migrant
Distance, speed and cost of the journey
Where (internal or international), why (voluntary or forced) and how long (permanent or temporary)
North, south and east

questions.question: A person who leaves Zimbabwe and settles in South Africa is called:
options: An emigrant in Zimbabwe and an immigrant in South Africa — one journey, two labels
An immigrant in Zimbabwe and an emigrant in South Africa
An internally displaced person
A commuter

questions.question: Mineworkers who spent eleven months on the mines and every December at home, year after year, practised:
options: Permanent migration
Urbanisation
Rural-to-rural migration
Circular or oscillating migration

subtopics.title: Push and Pull — Why People Move

questions.question: Push factors are best described as:
options: The attractions of the destination
The costs of the journey
The defects of the origin that drive people out
The laws controlling migration

questions.question: Chain migration means that migration streams widen over time because:
options: Governments recruit migrants in chains of contracts
Settled relatives at the destination provide beds, advice and job leads, making each next move cheaper and safer
Migrants are legally required to bring relatives
Transport companies lower prices every year

questions.question: Intervening obstacles in a migration decision include:
options: Transport costs, distance, visas and border posts, and the emotional price of leaving family
Only the weather along the route
The pull factors of the destination
The migrant's age

questions.question: People keep migrating into cities that already have severe unemployment because:
options: They are unaware that cities have jobs
Cities force them to come
Unemployment attracts migrants
They respond to an imagined destination — built from relatives' stories and photos — that is sunnier than the real one

subtopics.title: Case Study — Rural Eastern Cape to Gauteng

questions.question: The historical root of the Eastern Cape to Gauteng stream is that:
options: Gauteng has always had better rainfall
The homeland system packed people onto poor land while the migrant labour system sent men on mine contracts, with pass laws blocking their families
The Eastern Cape has no roads
Gold was discovered in the Eastern Cape

questions.question: The decisive pull multiplier drawing new Eastern Cape migrants to Gauteng today is:
options: Free housing provided on arrival
Cooler weather on the highveld
Home-village networks already established there, offering beds, advice and job leads
Shorter distances than to other cities

questions.question: For the Eastern Cape origin, the consequences of the stream include:
options: Gains of remittances and returning skills, but the loss of working-age adults, unploughed fields and grandmother-headed households
No gains of any kind
A younger population and more workers
Rising rural employment

questions.question: The stream is described as still partly circular because many migrants:
options: Move to a new city every year
Never send money home
Cross international borders monthly
Keep the rural homestead, send money monthly, return each December and plan to retire in the village

subtopics.title: Case Study — Crossing Borders into South Africa

questions.question: The main pushes behind the Zimbabwean stream after 2000 were:
options: Overcrowded cities and high rent
Hyperinflation that destroyed the currency, vanishing jobs and decaying services, compounded by political intimidation
Drought alone
A ban on farming

questions.question: The Zimbabwean stream is called MIXED migration because:
options: It includes men and women
It uses several transport routes
Voluntary economic migrants, refugees and asylum seekers travel the same routes together
It flows in both directions

questions.question: For sending countries such as Zimbabwe, emigration to South Africa brings:
options: Remittances that sustain families and the economy, but a brain drain of teachers, nurses and artisans that slows recovery
Only benefits with no costs
A rising number of skilled workers at home
Lower dependence on money from abroad

questions.question: The xenophobic violence of 2008 and 2015 is explained in the lesson as erupting where:
options: Migrants refused to work
Wealthy suburbs objected to new neighbours
Border posts were understaffed
Competition for scarce jobs, housing and services concentrated in the poorest neighbourhoods

questions.question: On the bus platform, the passenger who IS a migrant is the one who:
options: Travels furthest that evening
Carries a suitcase, a one-way ticket and a new address — because residence is about to change
Returns home by the weekend
Travels for work every day

questions.question: The two questions that sort every migration are:
options: How far, and how fast?
How expensive, and how dangerous?
Was a border crossed, and was the move chosen?
How old is the migrant, and are they employed?

questions.question: An asylum seeker is a person who:
options: Has fled danger within their own country without crossing a border
Has been refused entry at a border
Migrates seasonally for harvest work
Has applied for refugee recognition and is awaiting the decision

questions.question: In the tug-of-war picture, the four kinds of players on both teams are:
options: Money, people, safety, and land-and-sky factors
Trains, buses, taxis and planes
Youth, age, gender and language
North, south, east and west

questions.question: Every relative already living at the destination strengthens the pull because they:
options: Pay the migrant's full salary
Shrink the fear — a place to sleep and knowledge of who is hiring
Make the journey physically shorter
Remove the need for a job

questions.question: The "mud on the rope" in the tug-of-war stands for:
options: The pull of the destination
The migrant's family at the destination
Obstacles: fares, distance, permits, and the pain of leaving people behind
The weather at the origin

questions.question: In the villages of the former Transkei, monthly money transfers from migrants are often:
options: A minor extra income
Taxed away entirely
Spent only on luxuries
The household's largest income source — maize meal, uniforms, electricity

questions.question: What the remittance money cannot replace in the origin village is:
options: The absent working-age generation — unploughed fields, grandmother-headed households, clinics without nurses
The village's water supply
The school buildings
The taxi routes to town

questions.question: For the destination city, migration simultaneously:
options: Adds workers and removes all pressure on services
Supplies young workers, skills and new businesses, while straining housing, services and the bottom of the job market
Empties the townships
Reduces the size of the economy

questions.question: The four-box method for consequences questions is:
options: Four paragraphs about four different countries
Push, pull, obstacles, perception
Origin gains, origin loses, destination gains, destination strains — filled and attached to a named example
Four dates of migration waves
